cues.text: >> I'd like to thank everyone for joining today's DAU event.
It's another episode of our microelectronics series.
This is number one, semiconductors and systems 101.
My name is Emmett Simmons.
I'm the producer for today's event.
We also have David Pearson on as our host.
The agenda for today -- your microphones will be muted throughout the session.
The session is being recorded.
It will be posted to dau.edu/events, which is highlighted at the bottom.
Please submit all your questions via the chat, and we will verbally respond
to your questions towards the end of the event.
Your feedback is important to us.
There will be a survey.
We will post a link to the survey in the chat towards the end of the event.
If you're here for CLPs, the session does qualify for up
to 1.5 CLPs with supervisor approval.
They are not automatic.
You will need to apply for them, but there will be a CLP certificate at the end of the survey.
You can copy and paste the link.
So now, I'm going to turn it over to Dave to introduce our speakers.
>> Hey, thank you, Emmett, and thank you, everyone, for joining us today.
You know, microelectronics are critical to nearly all
of our modern defense and information systems.
If you've been following the press at all lately over the past few months,
you have undoubtedly heard about the impact these devices are having across our economy,
not just within the Department of Defense.
To help our defense acquisition workforce get up to speed on this issue,
we kick off today the first of a four-part series on microelectronics.
In today's session, our speakers will provide an overview of the series, and include discussions
on how microelectronics are designed, manufactured, and tested.
James Chew will get us started, and he is the chair of the NDIA Science
and Technology Division, and serves as a senior global group director for aerospace and defense
at Cadence Design Systems, the Silicon Valley-based technology company.
He'll be followed by Frank Schirrmeister, a senior group director, solutions and ecosystems
at Cadence, where he leads a team translating customer challenges in the hyperscale,
communications, consumer, automotive, aerospace/defense, and industrial
and healthcare vertical domains into specific requirements and solutions.
At the end of the presentations, we'll be able to have some time for questions,
so please submit them via the chat box, and I'll pass them on to our speakers
at the conclusion of the remarks.
Thanks so much for attending today, and let me turn it over to James to get us started.
>> Good morning, and good afternoon, everybody.
I certainly hope you all can hear me, and I certainly wish all of you a happy new year,
and I certainly hope that all of you and your families had a merry Christmas.
Thank you very much for the introduction, Dave.
I do want to make one little plug right here for our friends
at the joint strike fighter program office.
They, in fact, were the ones who asked us last year to develop such a course for them,
to help train the program managers who are executing the TR3 program.
Most recently, because of some work that we did with the joint strike fighter program office,
working with their performers, they were able to show the benefits of applying the principles
that you'll be seeing today to reduce the risk of the development of a certain TR3 systems.
What we're going to be talking about today is something --
I'm going to be sharing you my screen right now.
Hopefully, you all can see it.
Can you all see this?
>> Yes, sir.
>> Okay, wonderful.
Okay. So what I want to talk about today is that this is actually something
that we've been talking about as really digital microelectronics engineering.
And because, typically, when there's a lot of people talking about a subject,
you find out that it can rapidly turn into a buzzword that could be misinterpreted
and misunderstood rather quickly.
We want to tell you that digital microelectronics engineering has been a
commercial industry best standard for about the past decade.
A lot of it is based on -- it's work that was initially developed by the Department
of Defense, but because the commercial industry found out they could make lots
of money turning what was the VHDL, the very high-speed integrated circuit program,
into today's electronic design automation industry.
Which is the basis of all the electronic systems that are currently developed
by the commercial folks, and soon by many of the defense industrial performers,
that happens to be something that has caught the attention of the folks
within the Department of Defense.
To give you an idea about how powerful the technologies that we're going to be talking,
the capabilities we talk about today, is that most recently,
when General Haight [assumed spelling] was still the vice chief, he gave a discussion
about how the -- how, in the requirements process, they were now requiring --
the joint chiefs were now going to require unfettered data access for all DoD systems.
In particular, they said they no longer wanted to have a situation
where joint strike fighters could not talk to F-22's.
I sat down with General Haight and staff, and now Admiral Gilbay's [assumed spelling] staff,
and explained, well, if you're going to do that, you've got to use that old DSMC.
Yes, I'm dating myself now, but I am a proud graduate of the DSMC/APMC course back in '96,
of using that old mantra, up front and early.
You can't just simply say, "I want unfettered data access."
You have to actually require -- this is what that means
in the discipline called digital microelectronics engineering.
A lot of the defense industrialist people will tell you, "Oh, we're already going digital."
Well, when you start looking back -- and we've been doing this now --
Frank and I've been working this market now for six years.
When you start talking about -- to them about what they mean by going digital,
you find that they're -- in many cases, they're very good first steps,
but they're hardly what was needed to actually get to the state that you all are going to want,
where you end up with systems that are built right the first time,
that are affordably sustainable, and agilely modernizable, even taking into account
with the long life cycles that the DoD systems have to have.
The important thing that we hope that you get out of this series is a good definition
of what is digital microelectronics engineering.
We also hope that you appreciate the fact that you, the DoD, have the resources
to execute these type of capabilities now.
You have them at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, and you also --
with the Air Force Research Laboratory Sensors Directorate.
And you also have it with the defense microelectronics activity,
which is at McClellan Air Force Station, the Sacramento.
Hopefully, you guys will learn those two names.
The Wright-Patterson Air Force Base that has an emulation, the design center that can be used
by the entire Department of Defense, and is currently being used by not only science
and technology programs, as you might expect, but also acquisition, operation sustainment,
and modernization programs, which I think will surprise you.
You have a capability called the defense microelectronics activity
at McClellan Air Force Station.
That recently has been put under the auspices of the undersecretary of defense
for acquisition sustainment, and will soon have a site certification,
being the center for innovation and technology excellence in microelectronics.
So you have two very powerful resources that actually have and are up to speed
on the capabilities that Mr. Schirrmeister and I -- we talk a little later today.
The other thing -- as I said, this is something that has been proven by program offices,
and there are current program offices that are using these capabilities in acquisition,
in operations, sustainment, and modernization.
So we hope that you will agree, at the end of these four sessions, that we will be able
to successfully communicate, at the end of these four sessions,
that this is no longer science and technology.
This is a state of the practice.
The DoD has this capability, and by implementing this capability, you'll not only be able
to meet the joint chiefs' requirement for unfettered data access,
but you'll be developing new systems
that will have significantly reduced operation sustainment and modernization costs.
So with that, we'll go through this front -- I know you've been staring at my good friend,
Norm Augustine's, face for some time now.
And it was really Norm Augustine, when he was secretary of the army,
who was noticing a very distinct trend about the DoD systems.
He was noticing that it was the DoD's dependence on electronics that was the root cause
of increasing the requisition and operation sustainment costs.
It literally was the content of electronics was getting more and more, but what he was finding
out is that, getting a linear increase
of capabilities via electronics was causing an exponential increase in terms
of acquisition, operation sustainment costs.
Which not only includes the hardware, but also the software, as you might imagine,
and that's how he ended up with his famous law that you --
this is what you probably know him most for, by his quote of, "By the year 2054,
the entire defense budget will purchase just one aircraft."
Well, how did the commercial electronic systems industry break this law?
If you think about it, many of you either were the recipient of, or were the givers
of electronic systems as Christmas gifts.
And if you notice that those new electronic systems had a linear increase in capability,
but they seemed to cost, if not the same, maybe even a little less.
Well, how did that -- and you noticed that, the moment that there was issues with --
you could call it with the operating system.
You'd call it 1-800-SOS-APPLE, or whatever customer service, and somebody was there
that was immediately to service that issue.
And you probably noticed that, within the first couple of weeks,
you guys also received an over-the-air software upgrade to address some of the issues
that the manufacturer had found in the first few weeks of having
that product in the consumer's hands.
How did they do that, and how can you guys use this within your jobs in your respective areas?
Well, they invested in a DoD technology, and I still think this could be a cruel hazing ritual
within the Department of Defense.
But when I was in the Pentagon, working for the director of defense research and engineering,
once of the things I was asked to do was review some of the final reports.
This happens to be a final report on a program that the Department of Defense invested
in the '80s, called the very high-speed integrated circuit technology.
To go back to the future, everything that you hear about semiconductors today,
back in the '80s, was said about memory.
If you think about it, if you look back at the news reports, it was the Japanese
who was eating our lunch in terms of memory.
No one could make memory better, faster, cheaper, and the Silicon Valley
in fact was starting to die on the vine a little bit
because of their dependence on Japanese memory.
What happened is that, with the investment from the Department of Defense
on this very high-speed integrated circuit technology,
and my good friend Mr. Schirrmeister will be talking about what it means,
in terms of electronic design automation.
That created a design language which allows people
to actually develop electronic hardware systems in a software state,
emulate them in supercomputers to ensure that that system will work as it's --
as it was designed to do, such that you have confidence
that you only make that piece of hardware once.
You have first-pass success, and the reason why everything's come together is that,
because you're designing the system virtually, all the other stakeholders
in there either support equipment, and software developers have access to that hardware,
where everything comes together, and you have hardware-software co-verified before everybody
nods and say, "Yea, verily, it's now ready to produce."
And you're able to have first-pass success.
There's a reason why people want -- and for the commercial people, the reason why it's great
that you all are -- advantage of the billions and trillions of dollars of investment
in this area is that, commercially, these guys, these companies who are using these tools,
such as the ones that we're going to be describing later, are facing two things
that most defense industrial-based contractors or program offices don't face.
First off, these guys don't make a dime until they actually produce a product, and in fact,
most of the time, they took out a bank loan to make that product.
So, again, there's some incentive there.
The second thing is that, no matter how hard people try, Christmas only comes once a year,
and by missing Christmas, that can be a fatal event for companies.
And if you look at the Silicon Valley and other areas
that have a heavy electronic systems-intensive companies, their roads are littered
with companies that didn't get first-pass success, and they missed Christmas.
So the stakes for these companies are rather high.
The DoD has put in a definition of digital engineering.
I guess that's one thing we do very well, and if you take a look at this definition,
it really is subject to interpretation.
It's a great definition.
It says, "Well, it's a digital approach, and it does design.
It does systems design and models through a continuum,
from concept to disposal," and here's what it is.
But the reason why we're getting so many definitions within the defense industrial base,
and even within the program office as to what is digital engineering, is that there's no "how."
And it's always good to try to follow an example of how it's done.
This is how it's done in the commercial electronics industry.
This chart was developed by our friends at NVIDIA, and if you look at it,
you'll notice that, in terms of definition, that's what that's -- called requirements.
That is done -- they set very hard requirements, and that's done by using digital twins,
and lots of conceptual designs to look
at what the market is doing before they start the process of developing these systems.
Everything is linked.
It's cloud-based.
You see how digital twins are developed, and those digital twins are used
for the software DevOps developers.
The digital twins are used for the system and subsystem developers,
and digital twins are pushed out for the trainers, operators, and maintainers.
That's what we mean by digital engineering, and that, in fact,
is captured in the previous definition.
And that's something to keep in mind.
Here's why people in the -- why the people who make a difference in the building,
and also on the Hill, are very interested
in implementing digital microelectronics engineering.
First off, you got firm, fixed requirements.
You're able to run a whole bunch of conceptual designs and preliminary designs
without having to build hardware.
Because you know what you're going to have before you build it, and in fact,
are able to do outstanding cost bases of estimates,
you actually will know how much this will cost.
The other thing that gives you the predictability of what is -- of the IOC and FOC.
What we discussed earlier, what's very interesting, is something that was discussed
when we had some people in the undersecretary
of defense acquisition sustainment group out in the Silicon Valley.
When they found out that there's no such thing as separate IOCs and FOCs, they found out that
when a product is launched, IOC/FOC is the exact same thing.
There is no -- and if you think about it, back in the day,
we used to have something called beta versions.
You don't hear about beta versions anymore.
The consumer is demanding first-pass success, and they really don't want
to be guinea pigs before they get it right.
And that's what these tools
that Mr. Schirrmeister will be discussing with you a little later.
You have a confidently secure design.
It's continuously monitored, and that's why you get operating system upgrades,
and things like that, to prevent not only some issues that people have been finding
within the consumer base, but also to ensure that it remains secure.
You guys do not -- if you think about how you demand things in a --
when you buy stuff with your own money, you really do not want to have a car
that only operates 57% of the time.
You want a car that operates 100% of the time.
You don't want a cell phone that operates 46% of the time.
You don't want a computer operates -- you know, anything other than 100%.
I think you get my point on that.
You also want it to be affordable, in terms of operation, maintenance, and sustainment.
Nobody wants to have a maintenance hog, and you also want to make sure --
and in some cases, it's almost transparent that there's an agile, on-demand modernization.
For those of you who have older cell phones, and I happen to -- I'm looking at one of mine,
my personal laptop right now that I've had for 15 years.
It's just automatically modernized with software updates.
So I make sure that everything works right, and I have the up-to-date stuff.
And you also want assured interoperability.
Those of you who buy certain computers, you want to make sure
that that thing is backwards compatible, and also forwards compatible,
and that's exactly what the stuff that we're bringing to the table.
It's all going to get down to this concept called digital twin, and that's why,
after we spoke with our good friend, Will Roper, the former SAF AQ, he was able to make
that statement, not only e-create before you aviate.
But he was bold enough to make the statement
that digital engineering not only will reduce development timelines,
but also save possible billions of dollars in maintenance and sustainment costs.
That's a proven fact.
This is the center that's out at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base,
and if you please e-mail Mr. Pearson, I will provide to you the point of contact out there,
to get more information on there.
But as I said, it's now being used on several pilot projects for acquisition, sustainment,
and modernization, and parts -- types of programs right there.
This is what the payoff is.
You know, this is, as we talked about a little bit, we also need to also make sure
that we acknowledge the difference between commercial and the Department of Defense.
Right now, if you take a look at the percentage of cost of a product life cycle,
for a weapons system, it's 10% in science and technology, and they develop something
that says, "Okay, we proved it could work, but we didn't reduce it to engineering practice.
But trust us, it will make a difference."
And then the acquisition people get it, and that's usually
when you start having your issues.
Because yes, it works, but we don't know to engineer with it.
So we have to learn how to engineer with it.
Unfortunately, it's by trial and error.
For those of you who are on the line
who work the operations sustainment, you know what happens.
The acquisition guys then toss it over to the sustainment folks and say, "There you go.
Have at it."
And that's why this wall of confusion is something that --
that's why we end up with this wall of confusion.
And now, this is where the majority -- not only does the depot folks, and --
have to learn how to -- have to learn how to maintain this thing after it's been developed,
but also in terms of modernization, especially with how long we keep our systems.
That becomes a major burden for the department.
In fact, I think that that's why over 70% of a system's life cycle,
weapons system's life cycle, is in the operation and sustainment,
and especially the modernization area.
This is how the department would like to move it to, which is a commercial model.
If you really think about it, your biggest part you want as the development costs and --
which could also be acquisition cost.
You don't want to have a maintenance hog.
You want to have something -- you don't want to have a maintenance hog or a garage queen.
You want to have something that can be agilely updated, and affordably sustained.
By the way, I think these charts will be made available to you, and as I said,
please in the chat -- we'd be happy to address any of the questions that you have.
This is something that just came out over the -- in December.
This is how the automakers are now trying to use over-the-air upgrades.
How would you get -- for those of you who are motorheads,
how would you like to have the capability that if you own certain Dodge vehicles,
and you want more horsepower, you can just download it, and put it in your car?
Or if you own a Ram truck, you can just download new software that'll give you extra
payload capability.
This is what they're doing, and it's all because of the previous concept of using digital twins.
So the commercial folks are using it.
They're using it on platforms that are an outstanding analog to department --
to the department's weapon systems, and I think that this is --
this kind of takes away a lot of the hopefully fear factor on using this.
It's not just cell phones anymore.
When we first started doing this about six years ago, I can tell you that people will all say,
"Yeah, this works on a cell phone, but I've got a platform."
Yeah, it'll work on a computer, but I have this.
Well, here is an automaker who is putting their money where their mouth is, where they're going
to be doing over-the-air software upgrades to increase the performance of their vehicles,
and it doesn't hurt that they can make a lot of money off of this also.
This is in the December 13th publication called "Automotive News."
I do encourage you guys to take it out, because you'll find out it's just not Dodge taking --
looking at it, but all the automotive OEMs are looking at this potential --
about this potential revenue stream.
It turns out Congress and the General --
Government Accountability Office are noticing this also.
Just so you know, myself and Mr. Schirrmeister, on a biannual basis,
brief the Government Accountability Office as to where things stand,
in terms of commercial digital microelectronics engineering, and how's the DoD transitioning it.
Well, if you really think about what digital engineering does,
and as we go through the lessons, you'll see why we say this.
It's knowledge-based acquisition.
No longer do you need -- do you need to have large design reviews,
where for all practical purposes, the program execution stops for five
to six weeks to assess where the program is.
It's a continuous project management, where you know where the program is.
You know where the problem spots are.
You know where to focus things.
I encourage you to take a look at this report, but if you take a look at this chart,
quickly shows that those acquisition programs that use knowledge-based engineering ended
up with a unit cost decrease, and with not that much of a schedule growth.
And you can see, results are for those that did not use these type of practices.
Here's the ground truth about the defense industrial base
and commercial digital microelectronics engineering.
First off, access is not an issue.
We know this because our company and our competitors sell
to all the defense industrial base, and also, by the way, there is now a company in this space,
in the electronic design automated space,
that has been granted trusted supplier accreditation by the Department of Defense.
So you no longer have to worry about, well, are they -- can I trust these folks.
The defense microelectronics activity say, "Yea, verily, these guys have put in the process
that we can grant them trusted supplier accreditation."
And you guys can look that up on the DMEA website, as to who those companies are.
There's also, if you really think about it -- cost plus fixed fee --
keep in mind, these are business.
It sort of discourages the use of these type of practices, because yea, verily,
the companies on cost plus fixed fee, they get paid if they do it right.
But from what we've observed, and what the observation is that, they actually get paid more
if they do it wrong, because they get paid to do over.
So when you're developing your acquisition programs, you might really want to look
at this cost plus fixed fee versus other options,
maybe like fixed-price incentive fee, and stuff like that.
The acquisition, operation, sustainment, modernization, and DMS program managers need
to be educated, and work pilot projects to gain the confidence of these techniques.
Not only is this training, but there are also lots of risk reduction programs
that are being executed, and we certainly hope that, when it comes time for you to take a look
at your programs, either acquisition, operation, sustainment, or modernization,
you all will take a chance on this.
You have an existing infrastructure within the DoD that you can leverage.
And at the end of the day, it's a team approach.
As I said, the industrial base has these tools.
They're just waiting for a requirement to use it, and I do believe that,
by working together -- and that's the best thing we could do.
You work together with the industrial base, co-develop policies, requirements, access,
standards that make sense, that will make life better for everybody here.
So this is what's being done right now, in terms of implementing these separate practices
within the Department of Defense.
We talk about training, which you're doing now.
We talk about confidence, target pilot projects.
I will say that the Air Force, and the Navy, and Space Force are all implementing processes,
projects there, as well as the Army.
In terms of policies, standards, and requirements,
it's now a time to really take a look at, and re-look at government purpose rights access.
I think it's time to put -- it's clear that to do --
to implement, to fully get the benefits of the capabilities that we're going to be discussing,
the government's going to have to bring that back.
And it has to be done in a fashion that the industrial base sees the benefit of that,
and they slowly but surely are doing it.
I talked about how you now have a full trusted flow, and not only --
and you have a group called the defense microelectronics activity that can serve
as consultants in the development of the requirements,
and in the project management of your systems.
But also, you have an emulation design center at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base
that has those same type of capabilities.
At the end of the day, this is a state of the practice.
It doesn't require any S&T to mature, and it's programs such as this that we hope that,
when you turn to your experts -- and I will tell you now, this is a capability
that you have a next-generation -- new generations come out every two and a half years.
Which means if there's somebody who hasn't worked in this industry for a few years,
they're already at least a couple of generations behind.
So that's something to keep in mind also.
This is what the modules are.
We'll be covering all of this.
Normally, I'd be introducing my good friend Dr. Paul McLellan, but instead,
it'.ll be my good friend, Dr. Frank -- Mr. Frank Schirrmeister.
And you will be hearing him for all four modules right here.
The first one is just basics.
What is this?
Then, secondly is just, what does this flow do, and how does it end up producing a system
on time and on schedule that delights the customer?
Then, we're going to talk about the heart of the matter, which is digital twinning.
And then, of course, at the end will be co-development and verification, where,
at the end of the day, it shouldn't just be you have hardware -- in the Silicon Valley.
You don't have hardware guys working separate from software guys.
You have them working together.
If you would like, there is a competency exam at the end of this training that,
once you complete it, and you successfully pass it, that will count.
You will receive a digital badge from Cadence that is an industry standard
on competency at the semiconductor 101 level.
That's all I have for right now.
I'd like to, at this point -- and I guess we're going to be waiting until the end for questions.
I'd like to actually turn this back over to my good friend, Mr. Frank Schirrmeister.
Frank, over to you.
>> Sure. This is Frank Schirrmeister.
Let me start sharing here my screen, and I'm --
there's nothing better than filling in for a friend.
Paul and I know each other for the last 25 years or so.
He sends his apologies.
He's, of course, chief editor at Cadence, running our Breakfast Bytes blog,
the daily news blog, and he's a veteran in the industry, has been, yeah,
involved in lots of roles over the last 25 years.
And he called in sick because he came down with a fever and everything,
and is really not getting in a presentable state today.
So we wish him all the best, and I'll fill in for him.
To give you, like, a feel, who's talking to you here, the accent is, of course, German.
I'm born and raised in Berlin, Germany, went to the Technical University of Berlin,
studied electrical engineering, financed my university time
with doing musical instruments development, like software development, developed a couple
of chips myself, was a project lead for several chip developments over time.
I have participated in several books with chapters, and I'm also having a not daily,
but monthly blog at semiconductor engineering.
I lead, as I was introduced earlier, the solutions and ecosystem aspects
at Cadence Design System Solutions, include in this case aerospace,
and defense, and automotive aspects.
So just so you can place me, what I'm actually doing, where I come from.
So I'm an engineer by trade.
This first section, and as James pointed out, you'll hear me for the other three sections,
for the next couple of weeks as well.
This first section is really an intro into the semiconductor design,
and its enabling technologies, which is electronic design automation,
and that's going into what we now call these days computational software as well.
It's really a combination of two portions these days, electronic design automation,
which is the set of tools, if you will, to develop chips.
A set of tool is then also the set of building blocks underneath, which you can license.
We call this in our industry IP.
That has nothing to do with patents in our case.
It's really the building blocks, the non-differentiating IP, things like a USB,
PCI and so forth, which really you want to, like a Lego block, buy and instantiate.
So our industry, Cadence Design Systems, and the industry we are in, has taken on a lot
of this intellectual property blocks as well.
And the EDA component is really giving you both the tools, the methodologies,
and the building blocks for building chip designs.
There are two main parts in EDA, which -- on the tools perspective of EDA,
which include the IC design itself.
So those are the sometimes rather beautiful layouts you see on the left-hand side here,
which some of them actually made it into the Museum of Modern Art and so forth.
The first X86 chip and so forth -- and the other component of EDA is the printed board design,
the PCB design, printed circuit board design, which is really taking chips,
and putting them on a substrate on PCB substrate boards.
Those are the boards you find in your systems, in cases when you open those.
And there's a new trend here.
We can talk about that a little bit more in the next section, which is that we are now
at a stage in the semiconductor, and electronics, and design world where a lot
of these PCB aspects, because of the complexity of rather large chips,
because chiplet integrations, where you have -- that's a term you might hear.
Where you take the raw die of a chip, and integrate multiple of those in a package.
One of the things which has defined the industry really for the better part of five,
six decades here is something called Moore's law.
Moore's law, postulated by Gordon Moore in 1979, was that the number of transistors incorporated
in chip will exponential double every 24 months, and you have bear in mind that, at the time --
this picture here comes from Paul McLellan's library.
At the time, in the '70s, you really had transistors just becoming mainstream,
so to speak.
So you have some of these electronic components from that time,
including rather large transistors here.
To give you an impression of what Moore's law is really about, is the original graph,
which Gordon Moore there has actually -- I've seen the print of the paper,
the original scribble he did, was really on this log scale,
the components per integrated function on the design.
And he postulated that, and the industry followed his call, so to speak.
The technology was able to continuously grow the numbers of transistors per chip,
and you see these here, just by virtue of the Intel processors, Intel and AMD processors.
And be aware, the scale here is a log scale, so that's really a doubling.
What that means, a doubling, if you are or happen to be in Santa Clara,
there's a fantastic museum at Intel Headquarters, which I've taken my family to.
And Paul took this snapshot here.
